items.followUp: Define oscillatory motion and give one example.

rubric.why: A definition must describe motion in both directions about the equilibrium position.
rubric.description: Defines vibratory motion as to-and-fro motion about a mean position.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for both the repeated to-and-fro motion and the mean position idea; accept equivalent wording such as equilibrium position.

rubric.why: A suitable example completes the definition.
rubric.description: Gives a valid example of vibratory motion.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any correct example.

modelAnswer: Vibratory motion is the repeated to-and-fro motion of a body about its mean position.
Example: the prongs of a tuning fork vibrate about their mean position.

items.followUp: A cyclist travels 120 m in 15 s. Find the cyclist’s average speed.

rubric.why: The correct relationship is needed to calculate average speed.
rubric.description: States the formula for average speed.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for average speed = distance ÷ time, or an equivalent formula.

rubric.why: The correct substitution and result show the calculation is completed correctly.
rubric.description: Substitutes the data and gives the average speed with its unit.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for 8 m/s; accept equivalent unit formatting.

modelAnswer: Given: distance, d = 80 m; time, t = 10 s.
Formula: average speed = distance ÷ time.
Substitution: average speed = 80 m ÷ 10 s = 8 m/s.
Answer: the average speed is 8 m/s.

items.followUp: State the difference between like and unlike parallel forces.

rubric.why: Like parallel forces are distinguished by their common direction.
rubric.description: States that like parallel forces act in the same direction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the same-direction property.

rubric.why: Unlike parallel forces are distinguished by acting in opposite directions.
rubric.description: States that unlike parallel forces act in opposite directions.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the opposite-direction property.

modelAnswer: Like parallel forces are parallel forces that act in the same direction.
Unlike parallel forces are parallel forces that act in opposite directions.

items.followUp: A body weighs 196 N. Find its mass if g = 9.8 m/s².

rubric.why: The relation between weight, mass, and gravitational acceleration is required.
rubric.description: Uses the weight–mass relation and rearranges it for mass.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for W = mg and m = W ÷ g, or an equivalent rearrangement.

rubric.why: The stated values give the correct mass and unit.
rubric.description: Substitutes the values and gives the mass in kilograms.

modelAnswer: Given: weight, W = 147 N; gravitational acceleration, g = 10 m/s².
Formula: W = mg, so m = W ÷ g.
Substitution: m = 147 N ÷ 10 m/s² = 14.7 kg.
Answer: the mass of the body is 14.7 kg.

items.followUp: Define work and state its SI unit.

rubric.why: Work requires a force to produce displacement.
rubric.description: Defines work in terms of force causing displacement in its direction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for stating that a force does work when it causes displacement in its direction.

rubric.why: The joule is the SI unit of work.

modelAnswer: Work is done when a force causes displacement of a body in the direction of the force.
The SI unit of work is the joule (J).

items.followUp: What is another name for a solar cell, and what semiconductor junction does it contain?

rubric.why: Photovoltaic cell is the other name for a solar cell.
rubric.description: Names a solar cell as a photovoltaic cell.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for the correct name.

rubric.why: A solar cell is made using joined semiconductor layers that form a junction.
rubric.description: Describes its construction as joined P-type and N-type semiconductor layers, commonly silicon.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for identifying the joined semiconductor layers or the P–N junction; accept equivalent construction descriptions.

modelAnswer: A solar cell is also called a photovoltaic cell.
It is made by joining P-type and N-type layers of a semiconductor, usually silicon, to form a P–N junction.

items.followUp: Name two machines that work on Pascal’s Law.

rubric.why: The principle explains how pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted.
rubric.description: States the pressure-transmission principle of Pascal’s Law.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for saying that pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted equally in all directions.

rubric.why: Hydraulic devices are practical applications of the law.
rubric.description: Names a valid application of Pascal’s Law.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for any correct hydraulic machine or system.

modelAnswer: Pascal’s Law is applied in hydraulic machines, where pressure applied to an enclosed liquid is transmitted equally in all directions.
Examples include the hydraulic press, hydraulic lift, hydraulic jack and hydraulic brakes.

items.followUp: Describe four ways to reduce friction in machines or when moving through a fluid.

rubric.why: Lubricants reduce direct contact and rubbing between surfaces.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for oil, grease, or another suitable lubricant.

rubric.why: Smoother surfaces have fewer irregularities that interlock.
rubric.description: Polishes or smooths the contacting surfaces.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for polishing or otherwise smoothing surfaces.

rubric.why: Rolling friction is less than sliding friction.
rubric.description: Uses ball bearings or rollers to replace sliding friction with rolling friction.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for ball bearings or rollers.

rubric.why: A streamlined shape reduces resistive friction in air or water.
rubric.description: Streamlines the shape of a body moving through a fluid.
rubric.how: Award 1 mark for streamlining or a suitable streamlined shape.

modelAnswer: Lubricate the surfaces with oil or grease to reduce rubbing.
Polish or smooth the surfaces in contact.
Use ball bearings or rollers to replace sliding friction with rolling friction.
Give bodies moving through air or water a streamlined shape to reduce fluid friction.
